title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.3, Knowledge Capacity Scaling Laws
authors: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li

findings.claim: Language models store at most about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, and int8 quantization keeps it.
findings.quote: we establish that language models can and only can store 2 bits of knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8, and such knowledge can be flexibly extracted for downstream applications.

quantities.condition: synthetic factual (biography) knowledge with sufficient exposures; GPT-2/LLaMA/Mistral-style models

findings.bears_on: Central capacity anchor: a knowledge-saturated model carries ~2 bits per parameter of extractable content.

findings.claim: Int4 quantization of a capacity-saturated model cuts its knowledge to 0.7 bits per parameter, while int8 loses nothing.
findings.quote: Quantizing to int8 does not compromise model capacity (even for models on the boundary of 2bit/param); however, quantizing to int4 reduces capacity to 0.7bit/param.

quantities.condition: after int4 quantization of a model at 2 bits/param
after int8 quantization

findings.bears_on: A saturated model needs more than 4 bits per weight to keep its 2 bits/param of knowledge, so b_w.pretrained rises as models saturate.

findings.claim: MoE models with 32 experts lose only 1.3x capacity per total parameter.
findings.quote: MoE models, even with 32 experts, only reduce 1.3x in capacity compared to the base scaling laws, despite using just 8.8% of the total parameters during inference.

quantities.condition: derived: 2 bits / 1.3 for an MoE with 32 experts

findings.bears_on: MoE weights hold somewhat less information per parameter, consistent with experts tolerating lower rates.

findings.claim: Mixing in junk data cuts the capacity for useful knowledge by up to 20x.
findings.quote: Junk data significantly reduces model capacity. As an example, with a 1:7 ratio of "useful to junk" training tokens, capacity for useful knowledge loses by a factor of 20 x, even when useful knowledge is exposed 100 times.

quantities.condition: useful:junk token ratio 1:7, useful knowledge seen 100 times

findings.bears_on: Models trained on web data may hold far less than 2 bits/param of useful knowledge, but the weights still encode the junk, so the total content per weight need not be lower.

findings.claim: Language models store at most about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even in int8, so a 7B model holds ~14B bits.
findings.quote: we establish that language models can and only can store 2 bits of knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8 , and such knowledge can be flexibly extracted for downstream applications. Consequently, a 7B model can store 14B bits of knowledge

quantities.condition: synthetic biography knowledge, 1000 exposures, GPT-2-style models

findings.bears_on: Ceiling: a K-sized update (8e7 bits) can carry at most ~0.6% of a 7B model's knowledge, so knowledge-heavy generational jumps cannot fit in one block.

findings.claim: Capacity drops to 0.7 bits/parameter in int4 and to ~1 bit/parameter with only 100 exposures.
findings.quote: Result 8: Quantizing to int8 does not compromise model capacity (even for models on the boundary of 2bit/param); however, quantizing to int4 reduces capacity to 0.7bit/param.

quantities.condition: int4 GPTQ quantization
100 exposures per fact (Result 4)

findings.bears_on: Rarely seen knowledge stores at ~1 bit/param, so small updates hold even less new knowledge than the 2-bit ceiling.

title: Aggressive Compression Enables LLM Weight Theft
authors: Davis Brown, Juan-Pablo Rivera, Dan Hendrycks, Mantas Mazeika

findings.claim: If decompression may include fine-tuning, LLM weights compress 10-100x beyond what inference-oriented quantization achieves.
findings.quote: We find that models are orders of magnitude (10-100x) more compressible than standard practice would suggest, when one allows for high decompression costs, in the form of additional finetuning.
findings.bears_on: The adversary's rate is lower than inference quantization's once a decoder may run training; that decoding is itself a training workload.

findings.claim: Vector quantization plus 1B tokens of recovery fine-tuning keeps Qwen2-1.5B within 1.6 MMLU points at 1.15 bits per parameter, where AQLM collapses.
findings.quote: Our method maintains reasonable fidelity at $1.15$ BPP, with only a $1.6\%$ reduction in accuracy on MMLU.

quantities.condition: Qwen2-1.5B, 1B-token recovery fine-tune (~0.01% of pretraining): MMLU 56.5 -> 54.9, C4 loss 3.28 -> 3.69 (Table 1)
Qwen2-1.5B: MMLU 56.5 -> 48.4, C4 loss 3.28 -> 4.27; random-init baseline 25.6 (Table 1)

findings.bears_on: With fine-tuned decoding, ~1 bit per weight keeps most capability of a small model.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities yes

findings.claim: At 7B with only 50M recovery tokens, the losses are larger: MMLU 70.5 falls to 65.5 at 3.01 bits and 48.5 at 1.52 bits.
findings.quote: For the larger Qwen2-7B model, our method achieves an MMLU accuracy of 48.5 at 1.52 bits per parameter (BPP), compared to 34.0 for AQLM, representing a difference of 14.5 points.

quantities.condition: Qwen2-7B, 50M-token recovery fine-tune: MMLU 70.5 -> 48.5 (Table 1)
Qwen2-7B: MMLU 70.5 -> 61.2 (Table 1)
Qwen2-7B: MMLU 70.5 -> 65.5 (Table 1)

findings.bears_on: At 7B scale, sub-2-bit rates are not yet at retained quality with small recovery budgets.

findings.claim: Llama-3-70B weights keep very low reconstruction error down to 0.1 bits per parameter, but this was not evaluated on tasks.
findings.quote: the latter of which maintains very low MSE down to $0.1$ BPP with almost no degradation.

quantities.condition: Llama-3-70B weight-space MSE only; no downstream evaluation (Figure 10 notes no full evaluations on Llama 3 models)

findings.bears_on: If confirmed on tasks, larger models could reach the ~0.1-bit regime where b_w enters the NCI bound; unverified.

findings.claim: The headline estimate is that an attacker could reach 16x to 100x compression with small trade-offs when expensive decompression (fine-tuning) is allowed.
findings.quote: attackers could achieve 16× to 100× compression with minimal trade-offs, reducing the time it would take for an attacker to illicitly transmit model weights from the defender’s server from months to days
findings.bears_on: Supports the draft's '16x-100x' attribution as the authors' estimate, but see the next findings for what was measured.

findings.claim: On Qwen2-1.5B, vector quantization followed by decompression training holds MMLU within 1.6 points at 1.15 bits per parameter.
findings.quote: Our method maintains reasonable fidelity at 1.15 BPP, with only a 1.6% reduction in accuracy on MMLU. Thus, our method is able to obtain 16× compression compared to the original model without reducing downstream performance.
findings.location: Section 4.2 (Results); Table 1 (Qwen2-1.5B, original MMLU 56.5; 0.58/1.15/2.03 BPP give 48.4/54.9/55.5)

quantities.condition: Qwen2-1.5B, MMLU 54.9 vs 56.5, after 1B tokens of decompression training

findings.bears_on: The only downstream-validated 16x result is on a 1.5B model, which puts the central measured b_w.pretrained near 1 bit per weight.

findings.claim: On Qwen2-7B with only 50M decompression tokens, 1.52 bits per parameter keeps MMLU at 48.5, 22 points below the original 70.5.
findings.quote: For the larger Qwen2-7B model, our method achieves an MMLU accuracy of 48.5 at 1.52 bits per parameter (BPP), compared to 34.0 for AQLM

quantities.condition: Qwen2-7B, MMLU 65.5 vs 70.5 (5 points lost) with 50M decompression tokens
Qwen2-7B, MMLU 48.5 vs 70.5 (22 points lost)

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: for FP16 Qwen2 at 7B the measured result near 10x (1.52 BPP) loses 22 MMLU points and only about 5x (3 BPP) is within 5 points, so '16x-100x for FP16 Qwen2 models' overstates what was shown at scale.

findings.claim: The 100x-plus end comes from reconstruction-error (MSE) curves on Llama-3-70B, without downstream evaluation.
findings.quote: the Llama-3-70B Pareto frontier obtains very high-fidelity compression down to 0.1 bits per parameter (BPP), representing a 160× compression. Note that we do not run full evaluations on Llama 3 models

quantities.condition: Llama-3-70B, MSE-based rate-distortion only, no downstream evaluation

findings.bears_on: DISCREPANCY: the 100x end rests on Llama-3-70B and Pythia reconstruction error, not on Qwen2 and not on capability retention, so b_w near 0.1-0.16 bits is a hypothesis, not a measurement.

findings.claim: Decompressing Qwen2-1.5B used 1B tokens of continued pretraining and fine-tuning, about 0.01% of its pretraining data.
findings.quote: We train for a combined $1$ billion tokens on these two datasets, comprising approximately $0.01\%$ of the Qwen2 pre-training data of $7$ trillion tokens.

quantities.condition: derived: 6 x 1.5e9 params x 1e9 tokens; decompression of pretrained weights, not of an update; about 9x Gamma

findings.bears_on: Aggressive weight compression is paid for in decode compute that already exceeds one block's Gamma at 1.5B, so low b_w and decode-within-Gamma pull against each other in NCI's U condition.

findings.bears_on: Without fine-tuning, about 1 bit per weight loses a lot, so pure PTQ does not reach sub-1.5 bits at retained quality.

title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
authors: Sehoon Kim, Coleman Hooper, Amir Gholami, Zhen Dong, Xiuyu Li, Sheng Shen, et al.

findings.claim: Sensitivity-weighted non-uniform quantization plus a sparse FP16 outlier set stays within 0.1 (4-bit) and 0.5 (3-bit) perplexity of FP16 on LLaMA.
findings.quote: This enables nearly lossless compression with less than 0.1/0.5 perplexity deviation from the FP16 baseline for 4/3-bit, respectively.

quantities.condition: 3-bit dense + 0.45% sparse outliers, average bits (Table 1); PPL within 0.5 of FP16
4-bit dense + sparse outliers, average bits (Table 1); PPL within 0.1 of FP16

findings.bears_on: Scalar quantization with outlier handling reaches ~3.2 bits at small loss.

title: Scaling Laws for Precision
authors: Tanishq Kumar, Zachary Ankner, Benjamin F. Spector, Blake Bordelon, Niklas Muennighoff, Mansheej Paul, et al.

findings.claim: Post-training quantization hurts more the longer a model is trained, to the point that extra pretraining data can make the quantized model worse.
findings.quote: For inference, we find that the degradation introduced by post-training quantization increases as models are trained on more data, eventually making additional pretraining data actively harmful.
findings.bears_on: Data-saturated weights carry more information per parameter, so b_w.pretrained rises with tokens per parameter.

findings.claim: A fitted law over 465 runs (up to 1.7B params, 26B tokens) puts the compute-optimal training precision at 7-8 bits.
findings.quote: to be around 7-8 bits when fitting our scaling law on runs with quantization done to integer type

quantities.condition: compute-optimal training precision (integer type), lower end; extrapolated from runs up to 1.7B params
same, upper end

findings.bears_on: Training below ~4-8 bits costs extra parameters, so low-bit training does not reduce information per useful parameter for free.

findings.claim: Below 4-bit training precision, models would have to grow more than 4x to keep the same loss scaling.
findings.quote: the race to low-precision training may have to stop before going below 4-bits, since this would force model sizes to become disproportionately (more than 4x) larger to maintain loss scaling

quantities.condition: training precision below which the required model size grows by more than 4x

findings.bears_on: Implies a practical floor near 4 bits for trained weight precision, and near ~1-2 bits per effective parameter.

title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for On-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration
authors: Ji Lin, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, et al.

findings.claim: Activation-aware scaling keeps Llama-2-70B within 0.1 perplexity at 4 bits and within 0.4 at 3 bits (group size 128).
findings.quote: AWQ improves over round-to-nearest quantization (RTN) for different model sizes and different bit-precisions.

quantities.condition: plus per-group-128 scales; Llama-2-70B WikiText2 PPL 3.32 -> 3.41 (Table 4)
plus per-group-128 scales; Llama-2-70B WikiText2 PPL 3.32 -> 3.74 (Table 4)

findings.bears_on: The production default (INT4 weights) is near-lossless; 3 bits shows measurable loss without vector codebooks.

findings.claim: Quantization error is dominated by a small set of salient weight channels; protecting about 1% of them recovers most quality.
findings.quote: Protecting only 1% salient weights can greatly reduce quantization error.
findings.bears_on: Information is unevenly spread across weights, so mixed-precision schemes beat uniform rates and lower the average b_w.

title: ParetoQ: Improving Scaling Laws in Extremely Low-bit LLM Quantization
authors: Zechun Liu, Changsheng Zhao, Hanxian Huang, Sijia Chen, Jing Zhang, Jiawei Zhao, et al.

findings.claim: At 3 bits and above, quantization-aware fine-tuning stays near the pretrained model; at 2 bits and below, the network relearns its representations.
findings.quote: Our findings reveal a notable learning transition between 2 and 3 bits: For 3-bits and above, the fine-tuned models stay close to their original pre-trained distributions, whereas for learning 2-bit networks or below, the representations change drastically.
findings.bears_on: Below ~2-3 bits, a low rate comes from retraining, not from compressing the original weights, so it costs training compute.

findings.claim: With quantization-aware fine-tuning, a 2-bit LLaMA-3 8B is 3.4 points below full precision in average zero-shot accuracy.
findings.quote: ParetoQ dramatically narrows the 2-bit quantization gap to full precision to just 3.4 points, outperforming the best QAT method by 5.7 points and the vector quantization method by 7.1 points.

quantities.condition: LLaMA-3 8B, QAT fine-tuning; average zero-shot accuracy gap 3.4 points vs full precision (AQLM PTQ gap 10.5)

findings.bears_on: Heavily trained Llama 3 needs QAT to be near-usable at 2 bits; PTQ alone loses ~10 points.

findings.claim: A ternary LLaMA-3 8B trained with 30B tokens of QAT is 5.6 points below full precision.
findings.quote: In contrast, ParetoQ requiring only 30B tokens and utilizing standard AdamW optimization with cosine learning rate decay, narrows the gap to just 5.6 points.

quantities.condition: LLaMA-3 8B ternary, 30B QAT tokens; average zero-shot gap 5.6 points

findings.bears_on: About 1.6 bits per weight at 8B costs ~5-6 points even with fine-tuning.

title: The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits
authors: Shuming Ma, Hongyu Wang, Lingxiao Ma, Lei Wang, Wenhui Wang, Shaohan Huang, et al.

findings.claim: Ternary-weight models trained from scratch match a same-size full-precision LLaMA in perplexity from 3B parameters.
findings.quote: It shows that BitNet b1.58 starts to match full precision LLaMA LLM at 3B model size in terms of perplexity, while being 2.71 times faster and using 3.55 times less GPU memory.

quantities.condition: ternary weights from quantization-aware training from scratch; 3B PPL 9.91 vs LLaMA 3B 10.04 (Table 1)

findings.bears_on: With training-time quantization, 1.58 bits per weight suffices at small scale; this sets the from-scratch rate, not a compression of an existing model.

title: BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report
authors: Shuming Ma, Hongyu Wang, Shaohan Huang, Xingxing Zhang, Ying Hu, Ting Song, et al.

findings.claim: A 2B ternary model trained from scratch on 4T tokens is close to leading full-precision models of similar size.
findings.quote: Our results demonstrate that BitNet b1.58 2B4T achieves performance on par with leading open-weight, full-precision LLMs of similar size

quantities.condition: 2B params, 4T tokens; benchmark average 54.19 vs Qwen2.5-1.5B 55.23 (Table 1); non-embedding memory 0.4 GB

findings.bears_on: Native 1.58-bit training survives heavy training (2000 tokens/param), unlike PTQ of heavily trained models.

findings.claim: The ternary model beats 4-bit post-training quantized versions of a comparable full-precision model.
findings.quote: BitNet b1.58 2B4T maintains stronger overall performance than the INT4 quantized versions of Qwen2.5-1.5B on the evaluated benchmarks.

quantities.condition: Qwen2.5-1.5B: bf16 avg 55.72, GPTQ-int4 52.15, AWQ-int4 51.17, vs BitNet 55.01 (Table 2)

findings.bears_on: Small, heavily trained models lose ~3.5 points under INT4 PTQ, consistent with PTQ getting harder as training grows.

findings.claim: Training keeps a bf16 master copy of the weights; the ternary weights are only the forward-pass representation.
findings.quote: The master weight of BitNet b1.58 2B4T, used for training only
findings.location: model weights list after the abstract
findings.bears_on: The weights updated during training are 16-bit, so the b_w a training block reads is not the 1.58-bit inference rate.

title: PV-Tuning: Beyond Straight-Through Estimation for Extreme LLM Compression
authors: Vladimir Malinovskii, Denis Mazur, Ivan Ilin, Denis Kuznedelev, Konstantin Burlachenko, Kai Yi, et al.

findings.claim: Better quantization-aware fine-tuning of codebook-quantized weights moves the size-optimal rate for Llama 2 down to 2.0 bits.
findings.quote: From this perspective, PV-tuning pushes the Pareto-optimal frontier for Llama 2 to 2.0 bits.

quantities.condition: Pareto-optimal bits/param at fixed model bytes, Llama 2 7B-70B, with fine-tuning on calibration data

findings.bears_on: With light fine-tuning, the size-optimal rate is 2 bits per weight.

findings.claim: A 2-bit 13B or 70B model matches the 16-bit model one size down.
findings.quote: a 2-bit 13B model outperforms any 7B quantization and is comparable with the 16-bit 7B model. The same holds for the 2-bit 70B model.
findings.bears_on: At 2 bits, the cost of compression is roughly one model-size step, an 8x saving in bytes for the same quality.

title: How much do language models memorize?
authors: John X. Morris, Chawin Sitawarin, Chuan Guo, Narine Kokhlikyan, G. Edward Suh, Alexander M. Rush, et al.

findings.claim: GPT-style models trained on random bitstrings memorize about 3.6 bits per parameter before saturating.
findings.quote: our measurements estimate that models in the GPT family have an approximate capacity of 3.6 bits-per-parameter.

quantities.condition: GPT-style models 500K-1.5B params trained on uniform random data

findings.bears_on: Upper anchor for the information a weight can hold; a reader never needs more than ~3.6 bits per parameter of content.

findings.claim: Doubling weight precision from bf16 to fp32 adds only about 0.3 bits per parameter of capacity.
findings.quote: Doubling precision from bfloat16 to float32 only increases model capacity from $3.51$ to $3.83$ bits-per-parameter.

quantities.condition: bfloat16 training
float32 training

findings.bears_on: Most of a weight's width is not information: of 16 bf16 bits only ~3.5 store content.

findings.claim: GPT-style models memorize about 3.6 bits per parameter (3.51 in bf16, 3.83 in fp32) before generalization takes over.
findings.quote: our measurements estimate that GPT-style models have a capacity of approximately 3.6 bits per parameter.

quantities.condition: random-data memorization, models of about 100K to 20M parameters
bfloat16 training

findings.bears_on: Upper ceiling for how much a small adapter can hold: <= ~3.6 bits per trainable parameter, so a 10 MB bf16 adapter (5M params) holds <= ~1.8e7 bits.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities wrong; corrected here: Values 3.6, 3.51 (bf16) and 3.83 (fp32) bits/param are right, but the random-data capacity runs use models of 100K-20M parameters (Table 1: 8.0e4-6.9e6), not 500K-1.5B, which is the range of all models trained, including the text/membership-inference experiments.

title: Pretraining Large Language Models with NVFP4
authors: NVIDIA

findings.claim: A 12B model trained on 10T tokens with NVFP4 GEMMs (16% of linear layers kept in BF16) nearly matches the FP8-trained baseline.
findings.quote: For instance, the model attains an MMLU-pro accuracy of 62.58%, nearly matching the 62.62% accuracy achieved through FP8 pretraining.

quantities.condition: derived: 4-bit E2M1 + one 8-bit E4M3 scale per 16 values (plus a per-tensor FP32 scale); 12B hybrid Mamba-Transformer, 10T tokens; 16% of linear layers in BF16

findings.bears_on: Forward weights at ~4.5 bits suffice for the longest public 4-bit training run.

findings.claim: Master weights, weight gradients and optimizer state stay in FP32 during NVFP4 training.
findings.quote: The main weights (stored by the optimizer), weight gradients (used for gradient accumulation across microbatches and across data-parallel replicas), and optimizer states are also kept in FP32.

quantities.condition: precision of master weights, weight gradients and optimizer states

findings.bears_on: Low-bit training does not make the updated state low-bit; the information a training step changes is held at 32 bits.

findings.claim: A 12B model pretrained on 10T tokens with NVFP4 GEMM inputs in forward and backward matches the FP8 baseline.
findings.quote: We validate our approach by training a 12-billion-parameter model on 10 trillion tokens – the longest publicly documented training run in 4-bit precision to date.

quantities.condition: derived: NVFP4 = 4-bit E2M1 + E4M3 scale per 16 elements; GEMM inputs in Fprop/Dgrad/Wgrad; MMLU-pro 62.58 vs 62.62 FP8

findings.bears_on: Forward activations and backward gradients survive 4.5-bit GEMM inputs in a long training run; supports central b_a near 4.5.

findings.claim: 16% of linear layers (first two and last eight blocks) stayed in BF16 for the 12B run.
findings.quote: keeping the first two blocks in addition to the final eight blocks (FFNs or Mamba-2, each has 2 linear layers) in BF16

quantities.condition: fraction of linear layers kept in BF16 at 12B

findings.bears_on: Some boundaries (near the output) need more bits, so a uniform 4.5-bit b_a is slightly optimistic.

findings.claim: Attention and communication paths were not moved to FP4; that is future work.
findings.quote: refining the methodology to quantize all linear layers without impacting convergence, reducing remaining high-precision layers, and extending NVFP4 to attention and communication paths.
findings.bears_on: FP4 training has not yet been shown for tensors sent between devices (the NCI boundary case).

title: Low-Bit Quantization Favors Undertrained LLMs: Scaling Laws for Quantized LLMs with 100T Training Tokens
authors: Xu Ouyang, Tao Ge, Thomas Hartvigsen, Zhisong Zhang, Haitao Mi, Dong Yu

findings.claim: Quantization-induced degradation grows with training tokens, and fits predict that 2-3 bit quantization will be badly damaging for models trained on 100T tokens.
findings.quote: In particular, performance degradation with 2-bit and 3-bit quantization at the unprecedented training scale of 100 trillion tokens is predicted to be severe
findings.bears_on: Suggests the low b_w.pretrained figures from 2023-era models will rise for more heavily trained frontier models.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities n/a

findings.claim: A 70B model shows over 20% likelihood loss under 4-bit GPTQ once trained on more than about 17T tokens (fit on Pythia 160M-12B).
findings.quote: For a 70B scale model, achieving a QiD greater than 0.2 (corresponding to likelihood decrease by 20%) under 4-bit quantization requires over 17 trillion training tokens.

quantities.condition: tokens at which 4-bit GPTQ of a 70B model passes QiD 0.2; extrapolated from Pythia fits

findings.bears_on: Frontier models trained on 15-40T tokens may need about 4 bits per weight for retained quality, raising the central b_w.pretrained.

title: QTIP: Quantization with Trellises and Incoherence Processing
authors: Albert Tseng, Qingyao Sun, David Hou, Christopher De Sa

findings.claim: Trellis-coded quantization takes Llama 3.1 405B Instruct to 2 bits with about 1 point lower zero-shot accuracy, though WikiText2 perplexity nearly doubles; 3 bits is close to lossless.
findings.quote: Table 8 shows results for Llama 3.1 instruct-tuned models, including Llama 3.1 405B. At all sizes, QTIP achieves strong results.

quantities.condition: Llama 3.1 405B Instruct vs Meta 'FP8' (16-bit attn / 8-bit MLP): WikiText2 PPL 1.70 -> 3.29; ArcC 61.6 -> 60.7, ArcE 81.4 -> 81.1, HellaSwag 67.1 -> 65.4, PiQA 83.8 -> 82.2 (Table 8)
Llama 3.1 405B Instruct: PPL 1.70 -> 2.05; zero-shot within 0.3 points (Table 8)
Llama 3.1 405B Instruct: PPL 1.70 -> 1.79 (Table 8)
Llama 3.1 70B Instruct: BF16 PPL 3.52 -> 5.08, ArcC 56.7 -> 54.4 (Table 8)

findings.bears_on: The largest public dense model holds most task accuracy at 2 bits and nearly all at 3, so b_w.pretrained at frontier scale is 2-3 bits.

findings.claim: On Llama 2 70B, 2-bit QTIP is better per byte than an ideal 4-bit model (WikiText2 3.87 vs 3.12 FP16 without fine-tuning).
findings.quote: With QTIP, 2 bit models scale better than theoretically optimal 4 bit models.

quantities.condition: Llama-2-70B, WikiText2 PPL 3.12 -> 3.87 (1MAD code, no fine-tuning, Table 3)

findings.bears_on: Confirms 2 bits as the size-optimal operating point for 2023-era 70B models.

findings.claim: Heavily trained Llama 3 models degrade much more at 2 bits than Llama 2, and quantizing one sensitive layer collapses zero-shot accuracy unless worked around.
findings.quote: In our experiments, we observed that quantizing layer 0 v of all Llama 3 70B variants (including 3.1, 3.3, and all instruct models) resulted in catastrophic collapse of zeroshot performance.

quantities.condition: Llama 3 70B base: WikiText2 PPL 2.59 -> 4.97, ArcC 60.5 -> 28.0 with layer 0 v quantized (Table 7)
Llama 3 8B base: WikiText2 PPL 5.54 -> 7.33, ArcC 50.2 -> 44.2 (Table 7)

findings.bears_on: Models trained on more tokens per parameter need more bits per weight, pushing the retained-quality rate toward 3-4 bits.

title: QuIP#: Even Better LLM Quantization with Hadamard Incoherence and Lattice Codebooks
authors: Albert Tseng, Jerry Chee, Qingyao Sun, Volodymyr Kuleshov, Christopher De Sa

findings.claim: Hadamard incoherence plus E8 lattice codebooks and fine-tuning make 3-bit models beat lossless 4-bit ones per byte, and keep Llama-2-70B usable at 2 bits.
findings.quote: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a 3 bit PTQ method has outperformed a theoretical lossless 4 bit model and also the first time a 2 bit PTQ method has offered similar scaling to higher bitrates.

quantities.condition: Llama-2-70B, WikiText2 PPL 3.12 -> 3.91 (ctx 4096, Table 4; QuIP gives 5.90); zero-shot ArcC 51.1 -> 48.7, PiQA 81.1 -> 80.3, Wino 77.0 -> 75.9 (Table 3)
Llama-2-70B, WikiText2 PPL 3.12 -> 3.35 (Table 4)
Llama-2-70B, WikiText2 PPL 3.12 -> 3.18 (Table 4)

findings.bears_on: Moves the size-optimal weight rate from 4 bits down to 2-3 bits for 70B models.

title: Run DeepSeek R1 Dynamic 1.58-bit
authors: Daniel and Michael (Unsloth)

findings.claim: Quantizing DeepSeek-R1's routed experts to about 1.58 bits while keeping attention, dense and shared layers at 4-6 bits gives a working 671B model at 131 GB.
findings.quote: managed to quantize DeepSeek’s R1 671B parameter model to 131GB in size, a 80% reduction in size from the original 720GB, whilst being very functional.

quantities.condition: derived: 131 GB x 8 / 671B params; Flappy Bird coding test pass@3 score 69.2% (single task, 3 seeds)
derived: 183 GB x 8 / 671B params (2.22-bit dynamic quant); score 91.7%

findings.bears_on: A frontier MoE runs at ~1.6 bits/param with degraded but real capability, and ~2.2 bits with little loss on this one test.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities derived-ok

findings.claim: Uniformly quantizing all layers to 1.58 bits breaks the model, so the low rate relies on keeping sensitive layers at higher precision.
findings.quote: Quantizing all layers to 1.58bits gets 0% on our benchmark
findings.bears_on: The achievable average b_w depends on mixed precision: a small set of layers stays at 4-6 bits.

findings.claim: Routed MoE experts hold about 88% of DeepSeek-R1's weights, so compressing them dominates the total.
findings.quote: This leaves ~88% of the weights as the MoE weights! By quantizing them to 1.58bit, we can massively shrink the model!

quantities.condition: share of DeepSeek-R1 weights in routed MoE experts

findings.bears_on: In MoE models, the expert weights set the average b_w, and they tolerate lower rates than attention.

title: To Compress or Not? Pushing the Frontier of Lossless GenAI Model Weights Compression with Exponent Concentration
authors: Zeyu Yang, Tianyi Zhang, Jianwen Xie, Chuan Li, Zhaozhuo Xu, Anshumali Shrivastava

findings.claim: Entropy-coding the exponents of FP8 language models saves 9.8-14.8% losslessly.
findings.quote: Language models achieve moderate but consistent reductions between 9.8% and 14.8%

quantities.condition: derived: 8 bits x (1 - 0.098); FP8 LLM checkpoints
derived: 8 bits x (1 - 0.148); FP8 LLM checkpoints

findings.bears_on: For models trained and released natively in FP8, the lossless rate is about 6.8-7.2 bits, lower than BF16's ~10.8.

findings.claim: DeepSeek-R1 (671B, FP8) shrinks losslessly from 623 GB to 530 GB.
findings.quote: This improvement stems from ECF8’s ability to reduce the model’s memory footprint from 623GB to 530GB

quantities.condition: derived: 8 bits x 530/623; DeepSeek-R1-0528 671B FP8 weights, bit-exact

findings.bears_on: Frontier-scale lossless rate for an FP8-native MoE: about 6.8 bits per weight.

findings.claim: Theory for alpha-stable weight distributions bounds exponent entropy at about 2.67 bits, giving a float-format floor of about 4.67 bits with a 1-bit mantissa.
findings.quote: Our analysis proves that the ultimate compression limit corresponds to a floating-point format of roughly FP4.67.

quantities.condition: theoretical: 2.67-bit exponent entropy bound + 1 sign bit + ~1 mantissa bit; keeps only 1 mantissa bit, so it is a lossy format floor, not a lossless rate for real weights

findings.bears_on: Suggests floating-point representations bottom out near 4.7 bits; going lower requires integer/vector quantization.

authors: Patrick Yubeaton, Tareq Mahmoud, Shehab Naga, Pooria Taheri, Tianhua Xia, Arun George, et al.

authors: Tianyi Zhang, Mohsen Hariri, Shaochen Zhong, Vipin Chaudhary, Yang Sui, Xia Hu, et al.

findings.claim: The 8-bit exponent of BF16 LLM weights carries only about 2.6 bits of entropy.
findings.quote: its 8-bit exponent field carries only about 2.6 bits of actual information

quantities.condition: entropy of the 8-bit BF16 exponent field of LLM weights

findings.bears_on: Locates all lossless slack in the exponent; the remaining 8 sign+mantissa bits behave as incompressible.
